draft.stem: A product analyst is designing an A/B test to check whether a new checkout button color changes conversion rate compared to the current color. Which statement correctly pairs the null and alternative hypotheses?
options: H0: the new color increases conversion; H1: the new color decreases conversion
H0: conversion rates are equal; H1: conversion rates differ
H0: button color has no effect; H1: the sample size was too small
H0: the test result will replicate later; H1: it will not replicate
draft.explanation: The null hypothesis states no difference between groups; the alternative states a difference exists. Assuming a direction beforehand, citing sample size, or referencing future replication all confuse the hypothesis statement with unrelated testing concepts.

grounding.note: Defines the null hypothesis as the no-difference default tested against an alternative hypothesis of an effect.

draft.stem: An analyst runs an A/B test comparing two checkout flows and finds p = 0.03 for the conversion difference, using a pre-set significance threshold of 0.05. What does this p-value mean?
options: Assuming no true difference, a result this extreme occurs about 3% of the time
There is roughly a 3% chance that the null hypothesis itself is actually true
There is roughly a 97% chance that the new checkout flow is truly better
The observed difference would replicate in about 97% of future repeated tests
draft.explanation: A p-value is the probability of a result this extreme or more so if the null hypothesis were true. It is not the probability that either hypothesis is true, nor a replication rate.

grounding.note: Defines a p-value as the probability, under the null hypothesis, of a result at least as extreme as observed.

draft.stem: An analyst checks an A/B test's results every morning and stops the test the moment p drops below 0.05, well before the pre-planned sample size is reached. What is the main risk?
options: The test loses statistical power but the false-positive rate stays the same
The true false-positive rate rises well above the stated 5% threshold
The novelty effect becomes stronger the longer the test continues to run
Multiple comparisons across metrics inflate the observed effect size unfairly
draft.explanation: Repeatedly checking results and stopping as soon as p dips below 0.05 (optional stopping) inflates the real false-positive rate far beyond the nominal alpha, since each peek is another chance for a false alarm.

grounding.note: Describes how repeated significance testing without correction inflates the overall false-positive rate.

draft.stem: A mobile app team wants to know whether sending push notifications at 6 PM instead of 9 AM increases the app's open rate. Which pair correctly states the null and alternative hypotheses for this test?
options: Null: the two open rates differ; Alternative: the two open rates are equal
Null: the two open rates are equal; Alternative: the two open rates differ
Null: the app is generally popular; Alternative: the app is generally unpopular
Null: the 6 PM rate is higher; Alternative: the 6 PM rate is lower
draft.explanation: The null hypothesis assumes no difference between send times, while the alternative allows the rates to differ in either direction. Option A reverses this framing, C ignores the metric being tested, and D presupposes a direction without justifying a one-tailed test.

grounding.note: Defines the null as 'no effect/no difference' and the alternative as the claim being tested against it.

draft.stem: An A/B test finds a statistically significant 0.2 percentage-point increase in conversion rate with a very large sample size. What should the analyst include when reporting this result to stakeholders?
options: Only the p-value, since statistical significance alone is sufficient
The practical business impact of the effect size alongside its statistical significance
A recommendation to ignore the result because the lift is small
The confidence interval, but only when the result is not significant
draft.explanation: With a very large sample, even a trivially small effect can be statistically significant. Honest reporting weighs whether the effect size matters for the business alongside the p-value, rather than treating significance alone as proof of a meaningful win.

grounding.note: Distinguishes statistical significance from practical, real-world importance of an effect.
